desc:
A binary tree is perfect if every node that is not a leaf has exactly two children and all leaves are at the same depth. A single node is a perfect tree.

For every node of the given tree consider the subtree made of that node and all its descendants. Return how many of these subtrees are perfect. The empty tree gives 0.

How trees are given. There is no tree type here. A binary tree is passed as an integer array in level-order (top to bottom, left to right), the same way LeetCode serialises trees. A missing child is written as -1, and every real node value is non-negative. The children of a missing node are not listed, and trailing -1 entries are dropped, so a non-empty array never ends with -1. The empty tree is [].

For example, [1, 2, 3, -1, 4] describes the tree on the left: the root is 1 with children 2 and 3, node 2 has no left child and has 4 as its right child, and node 3 is a leaf.

    1
   / \
  2   3
   \
    4

For tree = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] the answer is 4: the leaves 4, 5, 3 and the subtree rooted at 2 are perfect; the whole tree is not. For [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7] every one of the 7 subtrees is perfect.
constraints: The array follows the encoding above exactly (valid level-order, no trailing -1)
hints: Every leaf is a perfect subtree by itself. Think about which extra condition lets a larger node qualify.
A node's subtree is perfect exactly when it has two children whose subtrees are both perfect and of the same height.
Walk the real nodes from last to first, storing a perfect flag and a height for each; count the flags that are true.
editorial: A perfect tree of height h is two perfect trees of height h-1 joined by a root, and a single node is the base case. So node x roots a perfect subtree iff it is a leaf, or it has two children, both children root perfect subtrees, and those subtrees have equal height.

Compute heights and flags bottom-up in the level-order array (children come after their parent, so go backwards). A node with exactly one child is never perfect. The counter of true flags is the answer. This is O(n) time and space.
